title: QNAP QSW-M2130 2.5GbE and 10GbE Switches Shown
gist: QNAP unveiled two enterprise switches at Computex, the M2130 and PoE-capable M2130P, built on a single Realtek RTL9313 controller with 24x 2.5GbE client ports and up to 8x 10GbE uplink ports, reflecting 2.5GbE's shift into the new baseline for business client connectivity even as trade-show attention skews toward AI server infrastructure.

insights.claim: 2.5GbE client ports are becoming the new baseline for standard business Ethernet connectivity because falling controller chip prices and the ability to reuse existing Cat5e cabling runs remove the two main cost barriers to upgrading past 1GbE.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Signals a broad enterprise/SMB switch refresh cycle as PCs increasingly ship with 2.5GbE NICs, benefiting multi-gig switch vendors (QNAP, Netgear, TP-Link) over legacy 1GbE-only incumbents.
insights.quote: which, thanks to falling controller prices and the ability to reliably use existing Cat5e runs, is quickly establishing itself as the new baseline for bread & butter client connectivity

insights.claim: QNAP is positioning its two-switch M2130 lineup (plain M2130 and PoE-capable M2130P) as sufficient on its own to cover most of an enterprise's core networking needs, combining an affordable multi-gig managed switch with a PoE sibling rather than requiring a broader product line.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Shows QNAP expanding its competitive footprint from NAS/storage into general enterprise networking, competing more directly with dedicated switch vendors for SMB IT budgets.
insights.quote: QNAP should be able to cover a good chunk of an enterprise’s networking needs with just these two switches.

themes.theme: M2130 Switch Silicon and Bandwidth Design

insights.claim: QNAP built the M2130 around a single Realtek RTL9313 MIPS-based controller with 1GB of RAM and 12 integrated 10GbE MACs, splitting them six-and-six between the 10GbE uplink/combo ports and the 24 shared 2.5GbE client ports.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Demonstrates how a single merchant-silicon chip (Realtek) now covers both multi-gig client aggregation and 10GbE uplinks, a marker of ASIC commoditization that lets vendors ship cheaper managed multi-gig switches.
insights.quote: Internally, the switch is controlled by a Realtek RTL9313 controller paired with 1GB of RAM.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Internally, the switch is controlled by"

insights.claim: QNAP merged RJ45 and SFP+ into shared "combo" ports on the 10GbE uplinks so admins can choose copper or fiber backhaul per port without needing separate copper transceivers, while keeping dedicated SFP+ ports for longer fiber runs.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Lowers installation cost and complexity for buyers versus switches requiring dedicated transceivers, a concrete design differentiator in SMB switch purchasing decisions.
insights.quote: integrating RJ45 ports directly into the switch simplifies the process by making the transceivers unnecessary for copper cabling
insights.locator: paragraph on combo ports and transceivers

insights.claim: The non-PoE M2130 supports up to 60Gbps of aggregated 10GbE backhaul bandwidth via link aggregation, precisely matched to the 60Gbps needed to serve all 24 2.5GbE client ports at full line rate with no oversubscription.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Indicates QNAP engineered non-blocking client-to-uplink bandwidth, a technical selling point versus cheaper switches that oversubscribe their uplinks.
insights.quote: exactly matching the 60Gbps that 24 ports would need

insights.claim: The PoE variant M2130P sacrifices half the base switch's combo-port flexibility (2 combo ports vs. 4) because PoE cannot be delivered over fiber SFP+ links, forcing a fixed 10GbE port allocation and requiring a 455W power supply plus two extra cooling fans versus the base model's single fan.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Illustrates the hardware and thermal cost vendors accept to add PoE, informing buyers weighing a PoE switch's price/complexity premium against a plain managed switch.
insights.quote: The impetus for this appears to be QNAP’s PoE functionality – you can’t use PoE with fiber connections
insights.locator: PoE version section, paragraph on combo port loss

insights.claim: QNAP tiers PoE power delivery unevenly across the M2130P's 375W total budget: the first 16 2.5GbE ports are capped at 45W each, while the final 8 2.5GbE ports and the four 10GbE RJ45 ports get up to 90W (the PoE++ maximum), so admins must plan device placement around per-port power limits rather than treating all ports as equal.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete deployment constraint affecting which ports can host high-power PoE devices (e.g., PTZ cameras, high-power APs) - a point of comparison against switches offering uniform PoE++ across all ports.
insights.quote: The first 16 2.5GbE RJ45 ports have a 45 Watt limit, while the final 8 2.5GbE ports and the four 10GbE RJ45 ports have 90W limits – the maximum for PoE++.

themes.theme: AI Hype Crowds Out Mainstream Hardware Coverage

insights.claim: At the trade show, mainstream enterprise networking and storage hardware such as QNAP's new switches was largely crowded out of visibility by the industry's dominant focus on AI servers and supporting infrastructure, requiring noticeably more effort to find than in prior years.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A proxy for vendor and media mindshare/marketing resources skewing toward AI infrastructure even at shows where core enterprise IT products continue to ship, relevant to gauging attention (and possibly capex) allocation away from traditional networking/storage.
insights.quote: With all of the focus on AI servers and supporting hardware, you had to do a bit more digging than most years to find more mainstream components, but they were there.
